title: Move work to the branch it should have been on
summary: You wrote an hour of code on main by accident, before committing anything. Stash is the cleanest way to move it — and it works because a stash belongs to no branch at all.
mental_model: A stash records your changes plus the commit you were on, but nothing ties it to a branch. Popping it somewhere else is a three-way merge against that branch — usually clean, occasionally a conflict, never a copy-paste.
danger: Popping a stash that contains an untracked file the target branch already tracks fails outright. Stash moves changes between branches, it does not overwrite them.

write.content:
RPM = 1200
RAMP_SECONDS = 5


def calibrate(factor):
    """An hour of work, written on the wrong branch."""
    return RPM * factor

# Calibration notes

Measured against the reference impeller.

steps.title: Notice the mistake before committing
steps.why: You are on main, with a modified file and a new one that both belong on feature/pump-tuning. Nothing is committed yet, so this is a working-tree problem — the easiest kind to fix.
steps.expect: pump.py modified, calibration.md untracked, on main.

steps.title: Stash it with a message that says where it belongs
steps.why: `-u` includes the new file. The message matters more than usual here: you are about to switch branches, and a stash called 'WIP on main' tells you nothing when you come back to it.
commands: git stash push -u -m "pump calibration — belongs on feature/pump-tuning"
steps.expect: Clean tree on main, one clearly labelled stash.

verify.label: the stash says where it should go

steps.title: Look before you leap
steps.why: `stash show --stat` prints the shape of the change and `-p` the full diff, both without touching your working tree. Confirm this is what you meant to move, and that nothing in it collides with the target branch.
steps.expect: Two files in the stash, neither of which the target branch tracks under a conflicting name.

steps.title: Switch and pop
steps.why: The stash is not bound to main — popping it on the feature branch performs a three-way merge against this branch's content. It applies cleanly here because both branches share the same base version of pump.py.
steps.expect: Both changes land on the feature branch, and the stash list is empty.

verify.label: the work arrived on the feature branch
a clean pop consumes the entry

steps.title: Commit it where it belongs
steps.why: The whole manoeuvre took four commands and left no trace. main never saw the change, and history reads as though you had been on the right branch all along.
commands: git commit -q -m "Add pump calibration and notes"
steps.expect: Three commits on the feature branch, one on main, and no calibration file on main.

verify.label: the work is committed on the feature branch

steps.title: Several stashes at once
steps.why: The list is a stack: `stash@{0}` is the newest. You can apply any entry by name, in any order — useful when you have parked two unrelated experiments.
steps.expect: The older experiment applied by name, while both entries stay in the list.

verify.label: an older stash was applied by index
apply leaves both entries in place

steps.title: Clean up deliberately
steps.why: Restore the working tree, then drop what you no longer need. Stashes left lying around for weeks are the reason people distrust the feature.

verify.label: the misplaced work ended up on the feature branch
verify.hint: stash -u on main, switch, then pop

verify.label: main has exactly its original commit

pitfalls: A stash applied to a branch with different content is a three-way merge, so it can conflict. It is not a copy — read `git stash show -p` first when the branches have diverged.
An untracked file in the stash whose name the target branch already tracks makes the pop fail outright. Check with `git ls-tree` before switching.
`git stash` without `-u` leaves new files behind on the wrong branch, where they quietly get committed later.
Stash entries renumber every time you push or drop one. Never rely on a remembered index; check `git stash list` each time.
If the work is more than an hour old, prefer a WIP commit on a scratch branch. Stashes are invisible to `git log`, are never pushed, and are easy to forget.
cheatsheet: its full diff, untracked files included
